title: karma: the Gita's ch. 3 revisited · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna stories (the…
hook: a proud young graduate comes home, and his father hands him a glass of salt water
carry: salt is everywhere, and you can't see it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhakti road: Yashoda's rope, two fingers short, until Krishna let himself be bound by love. Today, the third road, jnana.

A young man named Shvetaketu comes home after twelve years of study. He's twenty-four, he's memorized the sacred texts, and he is, the Upanishad says, conceited, thinking himself very learned. You know this person. Maybe you've been this person, home from your first year of college. His father, Uddalaka, asks one quiet question. Did you ask for the teaching by which what hasn't been heard becomes heard, and what hasn't been understood becomes understood? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. So his father starts teaching, with things from the kitchen.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `A PROUD GRADUATE.` → `ONE QUIET QUESTION.`

segments.voice: This is the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the oldest and most important Upanishads. The father gives lesson after lesson, and one of the most famous uses salt. Put this salt in water, he says, and come back in the morning. The son does. Now bring me the salt. Shvetaketu can't find it; it's dissolved. Taste the water from the top, says the father. Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the bottom? Salty. The salt is everywhere in the water, and you can't see it anywhere. Then the father says the line this road is built on. That subtle essence is in everything; it is the real; it is the Self. And then three Sanskrit words: tat tvam asi. You are that, Shvetaketu. He says it nine times in the chapter. What does it mean? Here the great schools you met a few weeks ago part ways, and none is ranked. Shankara's Advaita hears plain identity: your deepest self and the ultimate reality are one, like the salt and the water's taste. Ramanuja hears it as the way a body belongs to its life: you exist in that, and for that. Madhva's school reads the same words differently again, and keeps the soul distinct. All three are Hindu readings of the same kitchen lesson. The jnana road is the road of seeing this, not just repeating it. Shvetaketu knew a lot of words. His father wanted him to taste the water.
screen: `SALT, DISSOLVED OVERNIGHT.` · `SALTY AT THE TOP, MIDDLE, BOTTOM.` · `THE SUBTLE ESSENCE IS THE SELF.` · `THE SCHOOLS HEAR IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Imagine a glass of water with salt dissolved in it: you can't see the salt, but taste it anywhere and there it is. Turn that picture gently toward yourself: is something present in every part of your day, your moods, your memories, the quiet between thoughts, without ever being seen? Don't try to name it; just notice the taste of being here, top, middle and bottom, and if you pray, rest in that as a prayer.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and on the jnana road the action is looking: Shvetaketu tasting the water until he sees.
Your line: salt is everywhere, and you can't see it. Tat tvam asi: you are that. That's day three hundred four.

screen: `DAY 304 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA — THE WHEEL OF OFFERING.`

howItsDone: Tat tvam asi from the Chandogya Upanishad is counted among the four mahavakyas, the great sayings of the Upanishads, and is studied and meditated on across Vedanta traditions, each reading it in its own way.

fork.setup: you're Uddalaka. your son is proud of how much he's memorized, but he's missed the point. how do you teach him?
options: give him another book to memorize.
put salt in water and ask him to find it.
tell him he's not ready and send him away.
fork.reveal: the father teaches with the kitchen: salt he can't see, but can taste everywhere. then: tat tvam asi, you are that.

original.note: Sanskrit: tat, that + tvam, you + asi, are. Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 and the refrain after it.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'you are that' is a vague spiritual slogan.
what it means: a father teaching his son, with salt and water, that the subtle essence in everything is his own Self.
what a scholar hears: one of the four mahavakyas; Advaita reads identity, Ramanuja a body-and-soul relation, and Madhva's school famously divides the words differently, as atat tvam asi.

chat.says: What was the salt in the water supposed to teach Shvetaketu?
options: Something unseen can fill everything. His father says that essence is the Self: you are that.
That real knowledge means memorizing even more sacred texts than he already knew.
That every Hindu school reads 'you are that' the same way, as plain identity.
chat.meaning: The salt is in every sip, unseen. Uddalaka says that subtle essence is the Self, and tells his son: tat tvam asi.

Shvetaketu.meaning: the young man home from twelve years of study

notes: Chandogya 6.1.2: Shvetaketu went at twelve and returned at twenty-four, 'conceited, thinking himself learned'; paraphrased. Confirm.
'Nine times in all': the refrain tat tvam asi occurs nine times (6.8.7 through 6.16.3). Confirm the count.
Madhva's reading 'atat tvam asi' (splitting sa atma atat tvam asi): stated in the trapdoor as 'famously divides the words differently'. Confirm this is fair to the Madhva tradition.
